reason: Functional: an expand toggle. The button already reads "Information For", so the chevron is decorative by context and no alternative text was written for it.
Functional: a link to the newsletters page. The envelope icon sits beside the visible text "Newsletters" and carries no alternative text of its own.
Functional: the W3C logo linking to the organisation home page. The SVG title names the destination rather than the mark, which is the exact pattern the root README gives as high quality.

Functional: the Wikisource wordmark links to the main page, so it is a linked logo. The alt is the bare project name and says nothing about the destination. The icon beside it is correctly aria-hidden.
Functional: the logo links to the site root. The alt is the brand name plus the word "Logo", which describes the image instead of naming where it goes.
Functional: the submit button of the site search form, so the sub-type is a form control rather than a toggle. The alt names the action the button performs, not the magnifier drawing.

Functional: a link to Harvard's Instagram. But the link already contains the visible text "Instagram" and the image is aria-hidden, so the correct alt here is empty. Repeating the adjacent text is the redundancy the criteria warn about.
Functional: opens the site navigation. The button carries its own text "Open Navigation Menu", so the hamburger is decorative by context and has no alternative text.
Functional: a badge linking to mediawiki.org. The alt transcribes an image of text and the statement it makes is what the link is for, unlike a bare brand name on a home link.
Functional: an icon that is the sole link to an EPUB export. The alt names the action and the outcome, including the caveat about Kindles. Long, but every word of it is useful.
Functional: the W3C logo links to the organisation home page. The alt is the bare initials. The same organisation ships "W3C homepage" on the same logo elsewhere, which is what good looks like.
Functional: an icon-only button that opens the country and language picker. The label names the action and the current state, which is exactly what the criteria ask of a control that announces state.
Functional: the accordion toggle in the federal site banner. The button's own text carries the label and the chevron has no alternative text, the same finding as fi-2615.

Functional: an enlarge icon linking to the file page. The image has no alt at all, so the name falls back to the link's title, which announces the raw file name. That is the failure mode the root README names explicitly.

Functional: a link to the NPR shop, an external destination rather than this site's root, so the proposed logo sub-type is wrong. The icon sits beside the visible text "NPR Shop" and carries no alternative text.

Functional: a menu toggle. The aria-label announces "Open Menu" while the visible text reads "Explore", so the announced name does not contain the visible label. Voice control users cannot activate it by what they see.
Functional: an icon that is the only link to the sister projects list. The alt names the destination rather than describing the Wikimedia mark.
Functional: a hamburger with role=button and aria-expanded that opens the drawer, so it is a toggle, not a logo. The aria-label names the action it performs.
Functional: the WAI logo linking to the WAI portal origin, so it is a linked logo. The SVG title spells out the initiative and names the destination.
Functional: the close control of the mobile navigation. The alt names the action rather than the X drawing, and there is no adjacent text to repeat.
Functional: an icon that is the sole link to a prepared Wikidata query, so it navigates rather than returning to a root. The alt names what the link opens.
Functional: the search launcher. The button's own text carries the label "Search" and no alternative text was written for the magnifier.

Functional: the search link in the site navigation. Two correct decisions: the icon is aria-hidden with an empty alt because the link already reads "Search", which is the redundancy filter working as intended.
Functional: the header logo links to the site root. The alt is the institution name plus the word "Logo", which names the picture rather than the destination.
The whole link carries hidden and aria-hidden, so nothing about it reaches a screen reader at all. It is not an announced control, and the icon has no alternative text either.
Functional: an icon-only button that opens the delivery ZIP dialog. The label names the action asked of the user, not the pin drawing.

Functional: the footer logo links to the site root. But the link's own text already reads "ADA.gov U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division" and the image's alt repeats part of it, so the announced result is redundant and the correct alt is empty.
Functional: an icon-only button that opens the shop checkout. The label names the action rather than the cart glyph.

Functional: a link to Harvard's TikTok. Same finding as fi-1881: the link already contains the visible text "TikTok" and the image is aria-hidden, so repeating it in alt is the redundancy the criteria warn about.

Functional: a link to Mozilla support, an external destination rather than a root, so the proposed logo sub-type is wrong. The SVG is correctly aria-hidden and the link's text carries the label, so there is no alt text to judge.
